title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space simultaneously
formal: Does there exist a computable compiler that takes any deterministic multitape Turing machine M to a reversible multitape machine R such that the following holds? For each M there are constants \(c_{M} \ge  1\) and an integer \(d_{M} \ge  1\) so that, on every input x on which M halts, R halts with the pair \((x,M(x))\), uses at most \(c_{M} S_{M}(x)\) tape cells, and takes at most \(c_{M} T_{M}(x)^{d_{M}}\) steps. R must not halt on an input on which M does not halt. Here \(S_{M}\) counts total storage including input and output, and \(T_{M}\) is at least the input length, as defined below.
definitions: Machines have a finite state set, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary input symbols and a blank, and a fixed finite number of tapes and heads. Each step reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols, and moves each head by at most one cell. The complete configuration includes state, tapes, and head positions. Reversible means the partial one-step function on configurations is injective. The input x is initially present with delimiters on one tape and all other tapes are blank. M has a designated finite binary output on halting. \(S_{M}(x)\) is the number of cells initially occupied or visited on any tape during that run, with a minimum of 1; input and output cells are included. \(T_{M}(x)\) is max(1,|x|,number of transitions). Apply the same storage convention to R. Its output tapes retain x and \(M(x)\), and all auxiliary tapes are blank on termination. The compiler must halt on every finite syntactically valid machine description; its own running time is unrestricted. Simulation here preserves the computed partial function, not every intermediate configuration. The overhead constants may depend on M but not on x.
answer_criterion: Prove that such a compiler and bounds exist, or prove that no such compiler can satisfy them for all deterministic machines. Both resource guarantees must hold simultaneously for the same reversible simulation.
why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

importance.reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.

context_blocks.text: Saving the input is necessary when the simulated function is many-to-one: reversible configurations cannot merge different initial inputs into one final configuration. Counting input and output storage prevents free external memory from changing the target.

Known general simulations occupy different parts of the time-space tradeoff. Polynomial-time simulations use more than linear space in general; a simulation with \(O(S)\) space can take exponential time. The requested conjunction does not follow from either result separately.

The compiler formulation makes the simulation uniform across inputs, while allowing machine-dependent constants. It is the polynomial-time, linear-space version requested here, rather than a demand for nearly linear time.

progress.text: Bennett proves reversible simulation in \(O(T^{1+\varepsilon})\) time and \(O(S \log  T)\) space for fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), among other tradeoffs.
Buhrman, Tromp, and Vitányi interpolate between low-space exponential-time and higher-space polynomial-time simulations.
Vitányi identifies simultaneous time and space efficiency as the main unresolved general-simulation question.
